More profligate of Nero's expenditures were gifts to court favorites and pets, already outlandish enough in Nero's teenage years to alarm his mother. When Agrippina heard that Nero planned to give 10 million sesterces to a Freedman, she had the coins piled in a heap so that her son could behold his extravagance.

Ever eager to defy his mother, he took one look at the pile and ordered it doubled, saying, "I did not realize I had given so little."

Ultimately more than 2 billion sesterces would be spent on such bequests, so much that Nero's successors tried (with little success) to get most of it back.

Source:

Romm, James S. "Matricide." Dying Every Day: Seneca at the Court of Nero. New York: Alred A. Knopf, 2014. Print.

Julia Tyler frequently visited Congress to listen to the debates and soon caught the eye of New York Congressman Richard D. Davis, a rather homely gentleman whom she called "an invincible old bachelor of 50."

It got so that whenever she appeared, Davis would leave the floor, to the amusement of the other Congressmen, hurry up to the gallery, and begin showering her with compliments.

One day she showed up wearing a lavishly flowered hat and Davis headed at once for the gallery. A few minutes later the vote on a minor bill came up and when the teller called out, "Mr. Davis," all eyes turned to the gallery.

"Mr. Speaker," Representative James I. Roosevelt announced, "Mr. Davis has gone to the gallery to study horticulture."

Trump does not have standing to sue Ted Cruz for ineligibility due to citizenship.

For Trump to have standing he would have to show that Cruz's inclusion on the ballot is in violation of the law and is causing him a cognizable injury. What the sheeple are forgetting, as was brilliantly illustrated by Bernie getting "berned" by the Clintons and DNC in New Hampshire and Iowa, is that the primary process is not subject to U.S. election law. It is simply a game controlled by the parties themselves and if the RNC failed to prevent Cruz from running in the primary for his questionable citizenship, then the issue simply isn't an issue...for now.

In fact, it is unlikely that Trump, as a Republican, would ever have standing to sue Cruz for this issue. He will simply never be in a situation (i.e. the general election) subject to U.S. election law where Cruz's presence in violation thereof caused him a cognizable injury. If Cruz wins the nomination, Trump will simply be another voter, like the rest of us, and a voter's ability to have standing to pursue Cruz's eligibility will be treated the same as Obama's was...non-justiciable (i.e. resolved by the ballot not the courts. There is only two scenarios that would allows standing to pursue this issue. The first would be a suit brought by the Democratic/Third party nominees in the general election against Cruz. Standing in this scenario would be doubtful because it would be speculative at best to prove injury that Cruz's inclusion on the ballot as a Republican would have injured the DNC/3rd Party nominee. In other words, Cruz was not likely to steal their voters. The second, and more likely scenario involves Cruz himself suing because he is prevented by certain states from appearing on their ballots due to the eligibility issue. Cruz sues the states to be included on the ballot citing the exclusion as an (obvious) injury based off an incorrect interpretation of the Constitution's eligibility clause.

The only party i can plausibly see Trump having standing to sue would be the RNC for allowing Cruz to appear on the ballot in the first place. While the standing issue would arguably be resolved, such a lawsuit would be subject to many other problems.
